newsitem.title: USA: Ex-Miami cargo rates volatile and down post boom.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Miami cargo rates volatile and down post boom.

text.p: Now that the busy holiday season is over for air cargo at Miami International Airport, rates are generally coming down and are more volatile, forwarders and carriers said in a Reuter survey survey.
Most rateginning ts are generally down, but a few of the carriers are beo follow their European counterparts and raise rates while dropping the fuel surcharge, forwarders said.

"For example, to some destinations, they will drop the 10 cents per kilo fuel surcharge and then raise the rate 12 cents to 14 cents," one forwarder said. Some are dropping the fuel surcharge with no rate increase, forwarders said.
Challenge Air Cargo, Miami and the TACA group of carriers from Central America are the biggest so far to raise rates and drop the fuel surcharge.
Now that the busy season is over, forwarders said rates are volatile. "We are getting spot rates for the day," one forwarder said.
"The flights are going down empty and coming back full of fruits and vegetables," one forwarder said.
"Everything is infinitely more negotiable," one said.
Rates to Sao Paulo eased just slightly to $2.01 from $2.05. Bogota, on the other hand was up a little to 63 cents from 61 cents, the survey showed.

Forwarders and carriers are looking forward to a busier than usual Valentine's Day airlift, which begins in late January through the first two weeks of February. Flowers come from Colombia, Ecuador and other Latin American destinations through MIA and from there are shipped all over the world.
"People seem to have a little more money to spend on things like Valentine's flowers," said one carrier.
Because there are so many northbound flights from flower producing countries, shippers look forward to two to three weeks of bargain basement southbound rates to those destinations.
"Last year we had rates of 10 cents a pound", one freight forwarder said.
Cold winter weather in the United States has caused the usual delays and problems getting freight to and from MIA. But this year so far has seen fewer problems than in the past, forwarders said.

"We had some delays with Gateway. They just couldn't get the trucks out of there," said one freight forwarder. Gateway 2000 Inc., the computer manufacturer is located in frozen North Sioux City, South Dakota.
Peru's asparagus season is in full swing and many fruits, vegetables and fish are being imported into the U.S. from Chile.
This month's survey adds rates for Chile for the first time. Chile was MIA's fifth largest trading partner in 1995 with $75 million in goods shipped, up 29 percent from 1994.

Chile's export promotion bureau called PROCHILE has said that Chile wants to double exports from the current $16 billion by the year 2005. And MIA officials say that imports from Chile, particularly perishables, are increasing rapidly.

One of Chile's biggest exports is salmon and other seafood. It also exports a lot of fruit including grapes, peaches, berries and cherries, Claudio Silva, vice president, Lan Chile's cargo division said.
Imports to Chile include the typical merchandise to South America: high technology, telecommunications and medical equipment and machinery.
Longer-term, some see increases in MIA rates tield to airport improvements.

"Rates ex-Miami will start increasing dramatically" as the rents and fees charged by Miami International Airport start to take effect," Eric Andrews the U.S. general manager for Colombian all-cargo Tampa Airlines said.
Landing fees, for example, jumped from $1.15 to $1.34 per 1,000 pounds of aircraft on Oct. 1.

That means landing fees for a Boeing 747 cargo aircraft, which weighs 630,000 pounds, will jump from $724 to $844 at MIA. For a company that has three times per week operations, that totals $18,720 for a year, a MIA official said.
For a 757 passenger aircraft the landing fee increases from $230 to $268, adding about $14,000 per year for a daily flight schedule, the MIA official said.
Rents for cargo space are as much as doubling as carriers move from ramshackle old buildings into new state-of-the art cargo warehouses.
These increased fees "have to be passed on to the importers and exporters," Tampa's Andrews said.
Although some airlines are challenging these fee increases, the modernisation of MIA is sure to increase costs and thus cargo rates, even if the challenges are successful.
Forwarders and other airlines are keeping a wary eye on the American Airlines pilot negotiations.
Although most discount the possibility of a strike, "it would be a huge mess" for MIA cargo if the American pilots did strike, one forwarder said.

American has tremendous frequency and good rates, forwarders said. American also carries a lot of mail. If American pilots were to strike, the mail would have to go on other flights, causing a ripple effect of tightening cargo lift.
Other passenger flights would be full and there would be little belly cargo space available.
"The freighter operators will be doing back flips," an executive with one passenger carrier said.

American Airlines carried more freight in and out of MIA than any other airline during the first nine months of 1996, according to statistics gathered by the Metro-Dade Aviation Department. American handled 148,935 tons through September 30, 1996.
-- Miami news bureau, 305-374-5013
